_about: Vetted sources for health and relationship facts. A post may only state a number or a research finding that is listed here. Each finding has the wording that is safe to use. 'observational: true' means say 'a link, not proof'. Add a source only after checking the paper itself (DOI, PubMed or the publisher's page). The entries marked from_marketplace are copied from intimova.ng's citations library (content/foundation/citations.ts in cgrade/intomova_marketplace) and must stay in step with it.

sources.cite: Herbenick et al., Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2009

findings.text: 52.5% of women had used a vibrator.
Women who had used a vibrator recently scored higher on most measures of sexual function, including desire, arousal and orgasm. A link, not proof.
71.5% of women who used vibrators reported no side effects, and the side effects that were reported were mostly rare and short-lived.

sources.cite: Reece et al., Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2009

findings.text: 91% of heterosexual men who had used a vibrator had used it with a female partner.
44.8% of men had used a vibrator.

sources.cite: Frederick et al., Archives of Sexual Behavior, 2018
sources.sample: 52,588 adults, including 24,102 heterosexual women and 26,032 heterosexual men

findings.text: 95% of heterosexual men said they usually or always orgasm when sexually intimate, compared with 65% of heterosexual women.

sources.caution: Use the 'usually or always' figures only. Don't mix them with the narrower 'always' figures some articles quote.

sources.cite: Herbenick et al., Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2014
sources.sample: Nationally representative sample of US women

findings.text: Women said they used lubricant to make sex more comfortable, more fun and more pleasurable, and to reduce discomfort or pain.

sources.caution: Don't quote a single 'X% of women use lube' figure from this paper: the abstract doesn't give one.

sources.cite: Muise et al., Social Psychological and Personality Science, 2016
sources.sample: Over 25,000 adults across three studies, including the US General Social Survey 1989–2012

findings.text: For people in relationships, well-being rose with how often they had sex up to about once a week, and not beyond that. A link, not proof.

sources.cite: Kalmbach et al., Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2015
sources.sample: 171 college-age women, 14-day sleep and sex diaries

findings.text: Each extra hour of sleep was linked to 14% higher odds of partnered sexual activity the next day.
Longer sleep was linked to greater sexual desire the next day.

sources.caution: Say 'higher odds', not '14% more likely'. Small sample of young women.

sources.cite: Capogrosso et al., Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2013
sources.sample: 439 men seeking help for new erection problems at one clinic in Milan, 2010–2012

findings.text: About 1 in 4 men (26%) who came to the clinic with new erection problems were aged 40 or younger.

sources.caution: One clinic in Italy. A later study from the same group found closer to 1 in 5.

sources.cite: Mallory, Stanton & Handy, Journal of Sex Research, 2019

findings.text: Couples who communicated more about sex reported better sexual function, including desire, arousal and orgasm. A link, not proof, and many of the effects were small.

sources.cite: Dorey et al., BJU International, 2005
sources.sample: 55 men with erection problems, randomised trial

findings.text: In a small UK trial, 40% of men with erection problems who did pelvic floor exercises with a physiotherapist had normal erectile function after six months.

sources.caution: Small trial run by the people who designed the exercises. Never say the exercises 'treat' or 'cure'. Always add: see a doctor about erection problems, because they can be an early sign of heart or blood-sugar problems.

sources.cite: Danish Environmental Protection Agency, Survey of chemical substances in consumer products no. 77, 2006
sources.sample: 16 sex toys screened, 6 tested for migration

findings.text: Jelly-type toys are made of soft PVC, which can contain up to 70% plasticisers, including phthalates.

sources.caution: The report found little risk at normal use, so don't frighten people. Use it to explain why 'body-safe silicone' matters.

sources.cite: Basson, Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy, 2000
sources.sample: Review and model, not a survey

findings.text: A widely used model of sexual response describes desire that is often responsive: it can grow after closeness and touch begin, instead of arriving first.

sources.caution: This is a model, not a measured finding. Say 'researchers describe', never 'studies prove'.

sources.cite: Muise, Giang & Impett, Archives of Sexual Behavior, 2014
sources.sample: 335 people in relationships, and 101 couples followed for three weeks

findings.text: Couples who spent longer being affectionate after sex (cuddling, talking, closeness) reported higher sexual and relationship satisfaction, and still did three months later. A link, not proof.

sources.cite: Lastella et al., Frontiers in Public Health, 2019

findings.text: 70.8% said sex with a partner and orgasm improved their sleep, and 54.1% said the same after masturbation with orgasm. Self-reported, so it doesn't prove cause.

sources.caution: Say 'many people say they sleep better', not 'orgasm improves sleep'. Avoid the word masturbation on the slide; 'on their own' works.

sources.cite: Rider et al., European Urology, 2016

findings.text: Men who ejaculated 21 or more times a month had about a 20% lower risk of a prostate cancer diagnosis than men who did 4–7 times. A link, not proof.

sources.caution: Never 'prevents'. End with: see a doctor about prostate checks.

sources.cite: Atlantis & Sullivan, Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2012

findings.text: Low mood and sexual problems are linked both ways: each raises the risk of the other.

sources.caution: Mood posts end with a pointer to a doctor or mental health professional. Never say pleasure treats depression.

sources.cite: WHO estimate, 2017, as reported by The Guardian Nigeria and checked by Africa Check

findings.text: WHO estimated in 2017 that about 7.08 million Nigerians (3.9%) were living with depression.

sources.caution: Always give the year; the estimate is old.

sources.cite: Ojomu et al. (PMC3013270)

findings.text: In a study of 384 women in Ile-Ife, 63% had some form of sexual difficulty, and trouble reaching orgasm was the most common.

sources.cite: Nigerian FSD study, Enugu (PubMed 25385921)

findings.text: In a study of 500 women in Enugu, sexual difficulties were most common among women aged 41–50.

sources.cite: McCool et al., Sexual Medicine Reviews (PMC6013982)

findings.text: Across studies of 215,740 women worldwide, about 41% reported some form of sexual difficulty.
Sexual difficulties were more common where gender inequality is higher, reaching about 62% in some African regions.

sources.cite: Domain prevalence analysis (PMC8261092)

findings.text: Across studies, about half of women with sexual difficulties reported problems with lubrication (about 51%).

sources.caution: Check the paper before using: the marketplace label is generic. Hold the post until checked.

sources.cite: Cunha et al., Pharmaceutics, 2014 (PMC4190534)
sources.sample: 12 commercial lubricants tested in a lab

findings.text: Of 12 commercial lubricants tested, 7 were more concentrated than the WHO's recommended limit, and only 5 had a pH in the normal vaginal range.

sources.caution: Don't claim our lubricant passes unless the product page says so.

sources.cite: Althof et al., Sexual Medicine, 2014 (ISSM guideline, PMC4184677)

findings.text: Lifelong premature ejaculation (within about a minute, every time) is unlikely to affect more than 4% of men, far fewer than figures repeated online.

sources.cite: Cooper et al., Sexual Medicine, 2015 (PubMed 26468381)

findings.text: Simple techniques like stop–start have been tested in randomised trials. Two trials reported men lasting roughly 7–9 minutes longer than men on a waiting list, with no side effects reported.

sources.cite: Herbenick et al., Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy, 2018 (PubMed 28678639)

findings.text: Only 18.4% of women said intercourse alone was enough for them to orgasm. Most needed, or enjoyed, other touch as well.

sources.caution: Platform-safe wording: 'other touch', not anatomical terms.

sources.cite: Lindau et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2007

findings.text: 73% of adults aged 57–64, 53% of those aged 65–74 and 26% of those aged 75–85 had been sexually active in the past year.

sources.caution: These figures combine men and women; don't mix them with the by-sex figures some news reports give.

sources.cite: NHS, 'How do I use a condom?'

findings.text: Oil-based lubricants, such as lotion or baby oil, can damage latex condoms and make them more likely to break. Use a water-based or silicone-based lubricant instead.

sources.cite: NHS, 'Erection problems (erectile dysfunction)'

findings.text: Erection problems are very common. When they happen now and then, they're usually caused by stress, tiredness or drinking too much alcohol.
See a doctor if it keeps happening: it might be a sign of a health condition that can be treated, such as high blood pressure or diabetes.

sources.cite: Brook (UK sexual health charity), 'Painful sex'

findings.text: Sex is never supposed to be painful. Many people have pain during sex at some point, and causes include infections, anxiety and not enough lubrication. See a doctor or sexual health clinic.

sources.cite: Bello et al., BMC Public Health, 2025
sources.sample: 941 sexually active adults aged 18–45, face-to-face interviews
sources.checked: Checked on the source's own page on 30 Oct 2026.

findings.text: Of 941 sexually active adults aged 18–45 in Ibadan, 64.9% said they had ever masturbated: 69.9% of men and 62.4% of women.

sources.cite: Brook (UK sexual health charity), 'Masturbation'
sources.checked: Checked on the source's own page on 30 Oct 2026.

findings.text: There is absolutely no risk to your health from masturbation. You will not experience any permanent changes to your body as a result of masturbating.
Masturbation is not a betrayal of trust or the boundaries of a relationship.

sources.cautions: Brook names allergy to a toy or lube, and infection from sharing, as the only risks: add a care line.

sources.cite: WHO, UN Human Rights and UN Women, interagency statement, 17 Oct 2018
sources.checked: Checked on the source's own page on 30 Oct 2026.

findings.text: There is no examination that can prove a girl or woman has had sex. The appearance of a woman's hymen cannot prove whether she has had sexual intercourse.

sources.cautions: Sensitive in Nigeria: frame it as freedom from shame, never as an attack on anyone's faith. 'Hymen' is the source's word; keep it off slide headlines.

sources.cite: Veale et al., BJU International, 2015
sources.sample: Pooled studies of up to 15,521 men; erect length measured in 692
sources.checked: Checked on the source's own page on 30 Oct 2026.

findings.text: A review pooling studies of up to 15,521 men found an average erect length of 13.12 cm, measured in 692 men.

sources.cautions: No images. The abstract doesn't list countries.

sources.cite: Lever, Frederick & Peplau, Psychology of Men & Masculinity, 2006
sources.country: Online survey; the abstract doesn't name a country
sources.sample: 52,031 heterosexual men and women, self-selected internet survey
sources.checked: Checked on the source's own page on 30 Oct 2026.

findings.text: In one large online survey of 52,031 heterosexual men and women, 85% of women were satisfied with their partner's size, but only 55% of men were satisfied with their own.

sources.cautions: Self-selected, so not representative: say 'in one large online survey'.

sources.cite: WHO, 'Sexual health' (working definition, 2006)
sources.checked: Checked on the source's own page on 30 Oct 2026.

findings.text: WHO says sexual health requires "the possibility of having pleasurable and safe sexual experiences, free of coercion, discrimination and violence."

sources.cite: Zaneva et al., PLOS ONE, 2022
sources.checked: Checked on the source's own page on 30 Oct 2026.

findings.text: A review of 33 sexual health programmes found that including pleasure "can improve sexual health outcomes"; in the 8 that measured it, condom use rose.

sources.cautions: All were HIV and STI programmes, mostly for higher-risk groups: say 'in sexual health programmes', not 'for everyone'.
